newsitem.title: FRANCE: French producers urge change in EU chocolate plan.
newsitem.headline: French producers urge change in EU chocolate plan.

text.p: French chocolate makers urged European authorities on Thursday to harmonise chocolate production rules to allow the use of non-cocoa fats in chocolate everywhere in the European Union and not leave that decision in the hands of individal governments.

"A majority of members of the French chocolate makers association favours the use of vegetable fats in chocolate thoughout the European Union," Sylvain Margou, director general of the French chocolate makers Alliance 7 association, told a news conference.

Margou made the plea as three committees within the European parliament were reviewing a Commission proposal to allow up to five percent vegetable fats in chocolate across the EU, subject however to approval by individual governments.
The parliament as a whole is scheduled to discuss the proposal in January, Margou said.

Under a compromise reached in April the seven EU countries -- Britain, Denmark, Ireland, Sweden, Portugal, Austria and Finland -- that already allowed the use on non-cocoa fats in chocolate may continue to do so.
But a majority of EU states, notably France and Belgium have objected to the use of vegetable fats, saying it would hurt cocoa producers in developing countries.

Because the Commission's proposal is based on the principle of subsidiarity -- leaving it to individual governments to decide whether to allow the use of cheaper vegetable fats -- French chocolate makers said they stood to suffer unfair competition from producers in countries where use is allowed.

"The association regrets the lack of harmonisation on the use of vegetable fats other than cocoa butter, this situation exposes French companies to unfair competition from their European rivals," Alliance 7 said in a statement released at the conference.

Margou said chocolate manufacturers in France were hoping the current proposal could be amended in parliament to exclude the subsidiarity principle and allow the use of non-cocoa fats everywhere in the European Union.
If modified, the proposal would have to be submitted again to the European Commission for approval, further extending an already lengthy process, he said.

The Commission's proposal put forward after three-and-a-half years of argument, also said that if non-cocoa fats were used, the product could be called chocolate but would have to carry "clear, neutral and objective labels".
Cocoa producers and development groups have said the Commission's proposal could result in cocoa demand falling by up to 200,000 tonnes,
But a study by the Free University of Amsterdam recently concluded that only 33,000 tonnes of cocoa beans, or 1.3 percent of world demand, would be substituted.
